title: From Fan-Out to Fast: Sub-100ms API Design in Distributed Systems
gist: QCon London talk transcript in which eBay staff engineer Saranya Vedagiri lays out how to keep distributed APIs under 100ms: assign per-hop latency budgets, hunt hidden latency (network hops, serialization, cold caches, retries, thread contention), size thread pools by workload, cache with deliberate invalidation and data classification, contain failures with circuit breakers and fallbacks, and measure via p99 dashboards, tracing and SLOs. A key anecdote: green p95 dashboards hid a client-specific ~1% timeout problem, fixed by payload reduction, retry discipline and per-downstream thread pools.

insights.claim: Saranya Vedagiri argues that building a low-latency system once is doable, but keeping it fast continuously requires sustained engineering and a repeatable process, with no quick shortcuts.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Latency is an ongoing operating cost, not a one-off project; teams need dedicated performance discipline.
insights.quote: building a low latency system is doable once, but if you have to keep it the way that it is always, then it needs a lot of engineering.
insights.locator: I'm a staff engineer at eBay

insights.claim: Latency drifts with scale even when code is unchanged: a 30ms service can jump to 60ms at peak and 120ms during a dependency wobble because of retries, thread contention and queuing.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Capacity planning must model peak and dependency-degradation scenarios, not average conditions.
insights.locator: Let's understand, what is the cost of a millisecond

insights.claim: A sub-100ms request budget can be split roughly as edge ~10ms (TLS, routing), gateway ~5ms (auth, throttling), application logic ~30ms, data access layer, and a 10-15ms reserve buffer for real-world delays.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Concrete template for allocating SLA across hops in API design reviews.

insights.claim: Vedagiri contends microservices are overused, with teams splitting work one service could do into four and forgetting the network hop cost; removing one hop can save more time than rewriting thousands of lines of code.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Service consolidation can be a cheaper latency win than code optimization.
insights.quote: removing one hop saves a lot of time than actually rewriting thousands of code.
insights.locator: This is where it can be done in a single microservice

insights.claim: Response serialization (JSON payload translation) is an often-overlooked latency component, explaining why application logic can be fast while the API is slow; internal service-to-service calls may benefit from gRPC while public REST APIs use JSON, and GraphQL can tailor read payloads per client.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Protocol and payload choices are latency levers on high-fanout APIs.

insights.claim: Hidden latency sources include cold caches falling back to the database, untuned query shapes, queuing and thread contention that snowball with retries, total SLA bound by the slowest downstream, and excessive logging/tracing overhead.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Checklist for diagnosing tail latency in distributed services.
insights.locator: Cold caches. What if there is a cache miss

insights.claim: At eBay, p95 dashboards were green while a client saw timeouts: a failure under 1% of eBay's billions of calls was nearly 1% of that client's millions, which matters greatly for checkout flows where every transaction counts.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Aggregate percentiles can mask concentrated client-level failure; monitor per-client p99.
insights.quote: The p95 was looking fine, but the users still timed out.

insights.claim: Retry amplification is a hidden tail-latency cause: escalating retry timeouts (500ms then 1,000ms) make low-latency targets impossible, whereas for a Redis cache that usually answers in ~5ms, capping at 8-10ms and retrying (possibly hitting a different pod) works better.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Aggressive, tight retry timeouts beat long waits for latency-sensitive paths.
insights.locator: There can be so many causes which is not really evident

insights.claim: eBay fixed its timeout issue with three changes: payload reduction (a user map with thousands of keys returned to 400-plus applications that needed only 5-10 keys), retry discipline (retry only idempotent calls, with capped limits), and separate thread pools per downstream.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Over-fetching payloads to hundreds of consumers is a concrete, common latency tax.
insights.locator: Maybe you are reaching a different pod

themes.theme: Thread pools, caching and resilience trade-offs

insights.claim: Thread pool sizing should follow workload type: CPU-bound work about one thread per core (8 on 8 cores), I/O-bound work cores x (1 + wait/service time), e.g. 8 x (1 + 80/20) = 40 threads, with Little's Law (50ms x 500 rps = 25 concurrent requests) as a starting concurrency estimate before tuning.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Gives a defensible starting point for concurrency configuration; misconfiguration drives queueing collapse.
insights.locator: Now, having this right configuration is very important

insights.claim: Beyond thread pool size, services need right-sized queues and a deliberate rejection policy (outright reject vs shedding low-priority work) for when both pool and queue are full.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Explicit load-shedding policy is a resilience requirement, not an afterthought.
insights.locator: Once you have set some number with your thread pool

insights.claim: Caching trades roughly 5ms vs 30ms latency but needs multi-level design, small payloads of a few KB, and deliberate invalidation (TTL first, then event-based; version-based only with reliable versioning; stale-while-revalidate only where clients tolerate staleness), never caching price for checkout.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Cache correctness, not just hit rate, determines whether latency wins are usable in commerce flows.

insights.claim: Cacheable data depends on classification: public listing data is fine, internal IDs need InfoSec review, confidential PII must be encrypted/tokenized with decryption cost accepted, and classified data like SSNs or passport numbers must never be cached.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Compliance constraints limit latency optimizations, especially in financial contexts.
insights.locator: You know that you want to cache

insights.claim: Circuit breakers contain a failing downstream so queue build-up and retries do not cause a self-inflicted system-wide outage, while fallbacks (e.g. generic 'many people are viewing' text instead of exact counts) keep pages working when non-critical services fail.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Graceful degradation protects revenue paths when ancillary services fail.
insights.locator: Next, we'll move on to circuit breakers

insights.claim: Data partitioning should use generic keys like user ID rather than grouping hot sellers into one shard, since seasonal events such as US Thanksgiving would concentrate traffic; region-based sharding for regulation (EU vs US) still needs sub-partitioning.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Hotspot-aware partitioning matters most during peak retail seasons.
insights.locator: The other one is data partitioning

insights.claim: Tracing explains why problems happen while metrics show when; SLIs (success rate, latency within 200ms) roll into SLOs such as 99.9% monthly availability, and burning a month's error budget within a week should pause velocity work to fix the system.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Error-budget governance ties reliability to roadmap prioritization.

insights.claim: Load-test numbers from staging should not be used as production benchmarks; instead roll out at 1-2% of traffic or, better, mirror production traffic to compare new flows.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Production-traffic validation is the reliable path for performance changes.
insights.quote: Your environment in your lower region is not the same as what you're doing in production.

insights.claim: Vedagiri expects future latency gains from adaptive routing to less-loaded regions, AI-assisted prediction of hot cache entries for predictive warming, and edge-native execution.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Points to AI-driven infrastructure optimization as an emerging tooling category.
insights.locator: What is the future holding for us?

insights.claim: Her 48-hour playbook: pick one end-to-end flow, remove unnecessary or duplicate calls (including the shared dependency every flow calls), build a p99 dashboard, record per-hop latency, set budgets, then parallelize, add thread pools and caching, and compare before/after load-test results.
insights.speaker: Saranya Vedagiri
insights.so_what: Low-cost, immediately actionable process for teams to quantify latency improvements.
